slides.title: Build a grouped, outlier-audited evidence table

slides.teaching: Students open the Week 5 handout and predict the zone_summary numbers before running any cell — most should recall South > North from Meeting A without looking.

outcomes.head: Group and rank
outcomes.body: Group Radley Hall rooms by zone and by room_type, produce multiple aggregations, and sort the result.

outcomes.head: Flag, both ways
outcomes.body: Write and apply an IQR-rule function and a z-score-rule function to the same column.

items: Recall the grammar: group, aggregate, sort
Write and apply both outlier-flag functions

slides.teaching: Tell students the last agenda item is not optional practice — it is this week's graded assignment and the Project 1 milestone at once.

slides.title: Recall four terms from Meeting A before writing any code
rows: splits rows into categories before summarizing
flags values outside Q1 − 1.5×IQR to Q3 + 1.5×IQR
flags values where |z| > 2, z = (x − mean) / std
passes a function name in without calling it first
slides.callout: Grouping answers 'compared to what.' An outlier rule asks whether one row distorts that comparison. Today's studio uses both, first on Radley Hall and then on Project 1 data.
slides.teaching: Have students point to each term in their own Week 5 handout before Ctrl+Enter on the first real cell.

slides.title: Recall: groupby() exploded into four moves

parts.label: SPLIT by zone
parts.body: Collect North rows together and South rows together.

parts.label: APPLY + COMBINE
parts.body: Compute each group mean and return one Series.

slides.teaching: Have students name split, select, apply, and combine in order before moving on.

slides.title: Split, apply, combine - drawn
slides.alt: Diagram: one table of 24 rooms splits into a North group of 12 and a South group of 12, each passes through .mean(), and both combine into one row per zone.
slides.caption: One table in, two groups, one aggregation each, one summary table out.
slides.explainBody: groupby('zone') does the split. .agg() or .mean() does the apply. pandas does the combine for you, which is why the result has one row per zone rather than one row per room. Knowing which of the three you are looking at is how you debug a summary that came back the wrong shape.
slides.teaching: Ask what the output shape would be if the split were on room_type instead of zone - the diagram's middle column would have more boxes, and the combined table more rows.

slides.title: Build complexity only after the smaller part works

steps.label: ONE COLUMN
steps.head: Verify one summary
steps.body: Group by zone, compute one mean, and check it against Meeting A's headline number before trusting anything more complex.

steps.label: GROUPED SUMMARY
steps.head: Add aggregations and rank
steps.body: Multiple named aggregations in one .agg() call, then sort_values().

steps.label: OUTLIER FLAGS
steps.head: Write, then apply, both rules
steps.body: One reusable function per rule, applied first to energy, then to area, then to your own data.

slides.teaching: This sequence prevents students from debugging a groupby typo and an outlier-function typo at the same time.

slides.title: Predict: what dtype does this column show?
slides.question: What prints, on this course's real pandas install?
options: object — the classic pandas text-column dtype
slides.why: Verified against pandas 3.0.5: text columns now print as str, not the object older pandas docs might lead you to expect.
slides.teaching: This is the exact dtype line the next slide's df.dtypes call will show for room_id, zone, and room_type — confirm no one is thrown by str looking unfamiliar.

slides.title: Load Radley Hall and recall the trustworthiness interview
slides.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("building_rooms.csv")
print(df.shape)
print(df[["room_id", "zone", "room_type",
         "area_m2", "energy_kwh_m2_yr"]].dtypes)
slides.output:
(24, 12)
room_id                 str
zone                    str
room_type               str
area_m2             float64
energy_kwh_m2_yr    float64
dtype: object
slides.explainBody: Week 4 asked whether this data could be trusted. Today assumes yes, and asks a new question: compared to what — and does any one row distort that comparison?
slides.teaching: Confirm every student's working directory actually contains building_rooms.csv before moving on; a FileNotFoundError here stalls everything downstream.

slides.title: GroupBy object, defined
slides.definition: The intermediate result produced by df.groupby(col) alone — a plan for splitting rows into groups, not a finished table. Nothing is summarized yet: chaining an aggregation like .mean() or .agg() afterward is what actually runs the split-apply-combine sequence and produces a readable Series or DataFrame.

example.head: print(df.groupby("zone"))
example.body: Prints a line like <pandas.api.typing.DataFrameGroupBy object at 0x...> — a real, verified line from this course's pandas install, not a table of zone means.

slides.note: A GroupBy object is not a mistake to fix — it always sits between groupby() and an aggregation. Predict this exact print() on the next slide before you see it run.
slides.teaching: Ask what students expected instead — most beginners expect groupby() alone to already show North/South means; that expectation is exactly what this term corrects.

slides.title: Predict: what prints before any aggregation runs?
slides.question: What does this print?
options: A DataFrame with one row per zone, every column already averaged
A ValueError, because no aggregation function was given
slides.why: groupby() alone only plans the split — a GroupBy object, not a table. Chain .agg() or .mean() to compute anything.
slides.teaching: This is the single most common groupby() misconception — some students will confidently guess option A. Run it live immediately after revealing the answer.

slides.title: Recall from Meeting A: group, then aggregate
slides.code:
zone_summary = df.groupby("zone").agg(
    mean_energy=("energy_kwh_m2_yr", "mean"),
    mean_area=("area_m2", "mean"),
    n=("room_id", "count"),
).round(2)
print(zone_summary)
slides.output:
mean_energy  mean_area   n
zone                             
North        64.25      40.98  12
South       115.68      38.25  12
slides.explainBody: Run this first and confirm you get exactly Meeting A's numbers — North 64.25, South 115.68 — before Studio 1 asks you to build the same pattern for a new category.
slides.teaching: This is a deliberate checkpoint: any student whose numbers differ here has a data or environment problem to fix before Studio 1, not after.

slides.title: Studio 1: build the same pattern for room_type
slides.prompt: Group by room_type instead of zone, with the same three aggregations, then rank by mean energy.
steps: Write df.groupby("room_type").agg(mean_energy=(...), n=(...)).round(2).
Sort by mean_energy, descending.
Identify which two room types have n = 1 — flag them as thin evidence.
Write one sentence: does a single-room category deserve the same confidence as a 10-room category?
slides.teaching: Expected top of ranking: Server (410.0, n=1), Studio (94.0, n=6). Expected bottom: Closet (12.0, n=1). Both extremes rest on n=1 — press students to say so explicitly, not just report the number.

slides.title: Confirm the headline finding before building on it
slides.callout: South-zone rooms use about 80% more energy per m² than North rooms, on identical n = 12 and nearly identical mean area. Everything from here forward — ranking, outlier flags, decision sentences — should be read against this one finding.
slides.teaching: Ask one student to state the 80% figure from memory before you reveal the table — most should already have it from Meeting A.

slides.title: Recall: .loc[] and .iloc[], now doing double duty
slides.definition: df.loc[row_selector, column_selector] selects matching rows AND names which column to keep, in one call. Week 4 filtered rows only, with no column choice: rooms[rooms['zone']=='South']. The result keeps its ORIGINAL row labels — it is not renumbered from 0.

example.head: df.loc[df["room_id"]=="R306", "energy_kwh_m2_yr"].iloc[0]
example.body: Row selector: room_id == 'R306'. Column selector: 'energy_kwh_m2_yr'. .iloc[0] then pulls the one matching value out BY POSITION, whatever that row's own label is.

slides.note: .iloc[0] does not mean 'the row labeled 0' — it means 'the first value in whatever .loc[] just returned.'
slides.teaching: Write df.loc[condition, column] on the board next to Week 4's df[condition] — the comma-separated column choice is the only new part.

slides.title: Recall: tuple-unpacking, the pattern your function will use
slides.definition: A function that returns two values separated by a comma, like return q1 - 1.5*iqr, q3 + 1.5*iqr, packages them as one paired value — a tuple. Writing low, high = iqr_bounds(df[col]) unpacks that pair into two names at once, in the order they were returned.

example.head: low, high = iqr_bounds(df["energy_kwh_m2_yr"])
example.body: low receives the first returned number (18.25), high the second (134.25) — matched by ORDER, not by name.

slides.note: The names low and high are yours to choose — Python does not know which returned number is 'low.' Swap the two names and you silently swap which bound is which.
slides.teaching: Write low, high = 1, 2 on the board and ask what each name holds before running any real code — this is the exact pattern the next slide's iqr_bounds() function returns.

slides.title: Recall: the IQR rule, before you code it
slides.definition: Flags any value outside [Q1 − 1.5×IQR, Q3 + 1.5×IQR], where IQR = Q3 − Q1. A flag means 'investigate,' not 'delete' — the same convention Meeting A used.

example.head: iqr_bounds(df["energy_kwh_m2_yr"])
example.body: Q1 = 61.75, Q3 = 90.75, IQR = 29.0 → bounds (18.25, 134.25). Room R306 at 410.0 kWh/m²/yr sits far above the high bound — the room Studio 2 asks you to confirm.

slides.note: 1.5× is a convention, not a law of statistics — Meeting A named it as a stated, defensible judgment call.
slides.teaching: Ask students to recall these exact bounds from memory before showing them — most should still have 18.25 and 134.25 from Meeting A.

slides.title: Write one reusable IQR-flag function
slides.explainHead: One function, reused on every column
slides.explainBody: Recall the docstring and type-hint convention from Week 4: -> tuple[float, float] and -> pd.Series state what each function returns. Combining two Boolean Series needs & and | with parentheses around each condition — NOT Python's and/or from Weeks 2-3, which raises a ValueError on a Series. Write this once; Studio 2 through Studio 7 all call it, unchanged.
slides.teaching: Ask why iqr_bounds() is written as its own small function rather than inlined into flag_iqr() — because Meeting A's boxplot-bound discussion and this flag both need the same two numbers. Flag the &/| point explicitly: it is a real, common beginner trap.

slides.title: Studio 2: apply flag_iqr() to energy_kwh_m2_yr
slides.prompt: Confirm the function catches the room you expect from Meeting A.
steps: Add df["iqr_flag_energy"] = flag_iqr(df, "energy_kwh_m2_yr").
Print only room R306's row.
Confirm the flag is True.
State the IQR bounds you computed, in your own words, without looking back at Meeting A.
slides.teaching: Expected: True, with bounds 18.25 to 134.25. If a student gets False, the most common cause is calling flag_iqr on the wrong column name.

slides.title: Recall: the z-score rule, before you code it
slides.definition: Restates one value as 'how many standard deviations from the mean': z = (x − mean) / std. This course flags any row where |z| > 2 — some fields use 3; the threshold is a stated judgment call, not a universal constant.

example.head: z = (x - mean) / std
example.body: For energy_kwh_m2_yr: mean = 88.85, std = 72.54. Room R306 at 410.0 kWh/m²/yr → z = 4.43, far past |z| > 2 — the same room the IQR rule flagged.

slides.note: threshold=2.0 in the next slide's flag_zscore() is a default argument, not a hard-coded rule — a caller can pass threshold=1.5 or threshold=3.0 instead.
slides.teaching: Contrast the two rules once more before coding: IQR uses quartiles (resistant to extremes), z-score uses mean and standard deviation (sensitive to them) — that difference is why they can disagree.

slides.title: Write one reusable z-score-flag function
slides.explainHead: A default argument, doing real work
slides.explainBody: Recall default arguments from Week 3: threshold=2.0 is used unless a caller overrides it, e.g. flag_zscore(df, "area_m2", threshold=1.5). The rule's strictness becomes a stated, changeable parameter — not a hidden constant.
slides.teaching: Ask what would happen to R309's flag if threshold were raised to 3.0 — students should reason that 2.82 < 3.0, so it would stop being flagged, without needing to run it.

slides.title: Studio 3: apply flag_zscore() and compare with Studio 2
slides.prompt: Confirm the two independent rules agree on this column.
steps: Add df["z_flag_energy"] = flag_zscore(df, "energy_kwh_m2_yr").
Print R306's row with both flag columns side by side.
Confirm both are True.
Write one sentence: why does agreement between two differently-built rules increase your confidence more than either rule alone?
slides.teaching: This is the 'clean' case from Meeting A, now reproduced by the student's own two functions rather than watched as a demo — the point is that they built both tools themselves.

slides.title: Predict: do the two rules agree on room R309?
slides.question: R309 is a 120.0 m² gallery. Do both rules flag it?
options: Yes — both flag it, the same way they agreed on R306
No — the IQR rule flags it, the z-score rule does not
No — the z-score rule flags it, the IQR rule does not
slides.why: Verified: z = 2.82 flags R309, but area_m2 IQR bounds (−47.25 to 123.95) do not — same room, different verdicts.
slides.teaching: Most students expect the two rules to always agree after Studio 2-3's clean case — this is the moment that expectation breaks, on purpose.

slides.title: Now apply both functions to area_m2 — the rules disagree
slides.callout: IQR bounds on area_m2: −47.25 to 123.95 — wide because small offices and large studios both sit in this data, so even a 120.0 m² gallery fits inside. R110, a 3 m² closet, is not extreme enough by either rule. Same functions, same dataset, genuinely different verdicts.
slides.teaching: Walk through this as a guided reveal before Studio 4 asks students to reproduce it themselves — the point is that this disagreement is real, not a bug in anyone's code.

slides.title: Where the two rules part company
slides.alt: Scatter of room area against its z-score, with the z-score threshold line at 2 and the IQR high fence marked; R309 sits above the z line but inside the IQR fence.
slides.caption: Every room's area_m2 against its own z-score. Green line = the z-score rule. Amber line = the IQR high fence.
slides.explainHead: R309 lands between the two rules
slides.explainBody: R309 is a 120 m2 double-height gallery. The z-score rule flags it; the IQR rule does not, because this building's mix of small offices and large studios widens the interquartile range enough to swallow it. Neither rule is broken. They encode different ideas of 'unusual', and this room is where that difference becomes visible.
slides.teaching: Resist resolving this. The honest answer is that the room needs a human decision, which is exactly what Studio 5's keep/investigate/exclude sentence is for.

slides.title: Studio 4: reproduce the disagreement yourself
slides.prompt: Run your two functions on area_m2 and confirm the table above, then look for one more debatable row.
steps: Add iqr_flag_area and z_flag_area columns using your two functions.
Print the rows for R309 and R110 and confirm they match the table.
Sort the whole dataset by area_m2 and look at the 3 largest and 3 smallest rows.
Name one row, other than R309 or R110, whose flag status you find debatable, and why.
slides.teaching: There is no single correct 'one more row' answer here — grade the reasoning (relative to nearby values in the sorted list), not a specific room_id.

slides.title: Studio 5: write the keep / investigate / exclude decisions
slides.prompt: Write one sentence for each of R306, R309, and R110 — this is graded evidence, not a private note.
steps: Name which explanation (measurement error, genuine extreme, missing variable) applies to each room.
R306: justify KEEP, citing the server-room explanation.
R309 and R110: since the rules disagree or both miss, justify INVESTIGATE rather than a silent keep or exclude.
Save all three sentences in the cell provided — do not delete any flagged row from the DataFrame itself.
slides.teaching: Watch for students who quietly drop a flagged row instead of writing a decision sentence — deleting evidence is exactly the silent-exclude failure mode this exercise is designed to catch.

slides.title: Predict: is R306 still an outlier on area_m2?
slides.code:
df["iqr_flag_area"] = flag_iqr(df, "area_m2")
df["z_flag_area"] = flag_zscore(df, "area_m2")
cols = ["area_m2", "iqr_flag_area", "z_flag_area"]
print(df.loc[df["room_id"] == "R306", cols])
slides.question: R306 was True/True on energy. What happens on area_m2 (8.0 m²)?
options: True / True again — R306 is already established as an outlier
False / False — neither rule flags it on this column
True / False — only the IQR rule still flags it
False / True — only the z-score rule still flags it
slides.why: Verified: z = −1.11, and 8.0 m² sits inside the IQR bounds. Outlier status is never permanent — it depends on the column.
slides.teaching: Name the misconception directly: a flag is not a property of the room, it is a property of (room, column) together.

slides.title: The SAME row can be ordinary on a different variable
slides.code:
df["iqr_flag_area"] = flag_iqr(df, "area_m2")
df["z_flag_area"] = flag_zscore(df, "area_m2")

r306 = df.loc[
    df["room_id"] == "R306",
    ["room_id", "area_m2",
     "iqr_flag_area", "z_flag_area"],
]
print(r306.to_string(index=False))
slides.output:
room_id  area_m2  iqr_flag_area  z_flag_area
   R306      8.0          False        False
slides.explainBody: .to_string(index=False) prints a DataFrame slice without pandas' default row-index column — a cosmetic touch, not a data change. R306 is an extreme outlier on energy_kwh_m2_yr (Studio 2-3: both flags True) but an entirely ordinary room on area_m2 (both flags False, here). 'Outlier' always means outlier ON ONE VARIABLE — never a permanent label for a row.
slides.teaching: This is the model for the required transfer-safeguard check — the next slide asks students to turn exactly this comparison into their own assert statements.

slides.title: Studio 6: write your own transfer-safeguard asserts
slides.prompt: Prove R306's area_m2 status with 2-4 assert statements you write yourself — a different input than energy_kwh_m2_yr, which you already tested live.
steps: assert flag_iqr(df, "area_m2")[df["room_id"] == "R306"].iloc[0] is False.
assert flag_zscore(df, "area_m2")[df["room_id"] == "R306"].iloc[0] is False.
Add one more assert of your choice, on a different room (e.g. R110 or R309), on area_m2.
Restart the kernel, run the file from the top, and confirm silent, error-free output.
slides.teaching: This satisfies the course's required lightweight transfer safeguard: a self-generated check on a different input (a different column, R306 on area_m2) than the one worked through live in Studio 2-3 (energy_kwh_m2_yr).

slides.title: This studio IS your Project 1 checkpoint

steps.label: DATASET
steps.head: You already chose it
steps.body: In Week 4 you selected and cleaned your own Project 1 dataset. Today's pipeline runs on THAT file, not a new one.

steps.label: QUESTION
steps.head: Restate it here
steps.body: Write your Week 4 research question again before grouping — the grouping choice should serve that question, not the other way around.

steps.label: PROVENANCE
steps.head: This is the milestone
steps.body: A grouped/ranked table, dual-rule outlier flags, and decision sentences on your own data — submitted this week — IS the Project 1 dataset/question/provenance checkpoint. No separate memo is required.

slides.teaching: Say this explicitly and only once, clearly: nothing extra is owed beyond what Studio 7 produces. Point to Project 1 Part II in the syllabus if anyone is unsure.

slides.title: Studio 7: apply today's pipeline to your OWN dataset
slides.prompt: Repeat group → aggregate → sort → flag_iqr → flag_zscore → decision sentences on your Week 4 Project 1 dataset.
steps: Set DATA_PATH to your Week 4 cleaned CSV (it defaults to Radley Hall's file so this cell still runs before you edit it).
Set GROUP_COL and VALUE_COL to your own categorical and numeric columns.
Group, aggregate, sort, and print the ranked summary for your data.
Apply flag_iqr and flag_zscore to VALUE_COL, and write one keep / investigate / exclude sentence per flagged row.
slides.teaching: Circulate here more than anywhere else this session — column names, missing values, and group sizes will differ a lot across student datasets. The functions should not need to change; only the three variables at the top of the cell should.

slides.title: Studio 8: audit an AI-generated outlier function
slides.prompt: AI wrote a z-score flag function that only checks one direction and silently drops flagged rows instead of recording them.
steps: Explain why z > 2 (not abs(z) > 2) misses low outliers entirely.
Name the missing IQR cross-check this function never runs.
Rewrite the function so a flag is recorded in a new column, never deleted from the DataFrame.
Confirm the repaired function still flags R306 on energy_kwh_m2_yr.
slides.teaching: Show the AI code: def flag_outliers(s): return s[((s - s.mean())/s.std()) > 2]. Require evidence from a rerun, not just a claim the repair looks better.

slides.title: Submit a small, reproducible evidence package

steps.label: SCRIPT
steps.head: Runs top to bottom
steps.body: Restarted kernel, no leftover variables from earlier drafts.

steps.label: FLAGS
steps.head: Both rules, shown
steps.body: iqr_flag and z_flag columns for at least one numeric column, on your own data.

steps.label: DECISIONS
steps.head: One sentence per flag
steps.body: keep / investigate / exclude, naming measurement error, genuine extreme, or missing variable.

steps.label: DISCLOSURE
steps.head: AI-use record
steps.body: Tool, prompt, what you accepted, modified, or rejected, and how you tested it.

slides.teaching: Use peer verification before submission — one student runs the file from a restarted kernel while the other checks all four items against the screen.

slides.title: A flagged row is a question, not a conclusion
takeaways: groupby() + .agg() turns many rows into one ranked, comparable table.
flag_iqr() and flag_zscore() are two independent lenses on the same column.
Agreement earns confidence; disagreement earns a written decision, not a coin flip.
This studio's output is this week's Project 1 checkpoint — on your own data.
slides.teaching: Exit prompt: students state, out loud or in writing, which of their own dataset's flagged rows they are least confident about, and why.
